title: Why the two axioms are in the definition
promptMarkdown: In your own words, without the notes open, and in under 250 words: explain why the definition of a smooth manifold includes the Hausdorff axiom and the second countability axiom in addition to the existence of a smooth atlas. For each axiom give (a) one example showing that 'locally Euclidean with smooth overlaps' does not imply it, and (b) one consequence of the axiom that the theory will rely on (you may name results to come: uniqueness of limits, closedness of compact sets, partitions of unity, embedding in some $\mathbb{R}^N$, countable atlases).
hintLadder: Which of the two pathologies from lecture 2 violates which axiom?
What does a convergent sequence do on the line with two origins? What does 'uncountably many disjoint open sets' prevent you from doing with a cover?

criteria.criterion: Correct witness (line with two origins) and a correct consequence (unique limits or compact sets closed) for the Hausdorff axiom.

levels.label: not met
levels.description: Neither, or confused with second countability.

criteria.criterion: Correct witness (long line) and a correct consequence (partitions of unity, countable atlas or embedding) for second countability.
States clearly that the atlas alone does not give either axiom.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Stated and connected to the examples.
